verdicts.reason:
Both essays reach the same verdict: the training objective cannot settle whether self-reports track internal states, so the question is about mechanism and is answered by intervention. B gets there with more distinctive and more discriminating conceptual machinery.

A's best moves are (i) the selection-for/selection-of diagnosis of the debunking inference, (ii) Nozick-style method relativization, (iii) the thesis that genealogical debunking weakens as the target facts become causally integrated with the belief-forming mechanism, with self-report as the limiting case, and (iv) the M1/M2 point that 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' misspecifies the intervention. Much of (i) and (ii) applies well-worn tools from the evolutionary-debunking literature. A's positive criterion (intervention, content-match, non-observational route) also stays binary: a report either is or is not 'introspectively grounded.'

B contributes more original structure.
- It derives inherited allocation A_D(x) = Σ_s P_D(r|x,s)P_D(s|x). This shows precisely what corpus imitation can and cannot fix: allocation over prompts at a typical human's rate, with no term for the model's own state.
- It separates aetiology from causal grain and replaces the trained/tracking binary with four hypotheses. Two of these are distinctions A lacks: H2, dispositional self-theory, and H3, proxy monitoring. Each hypothesis gets differential predictions under concrete designs (stratification, sibling and observer comparisons, item-level editing, proxy dissociation).
- Its handling of the common-cause objection is sharper than anything in A. Because frequency can reach the report only through the network's computation, 'corpus frequency is a common cause' is not a rival to the mediation question but one answer to it. B also shows that representation-sharing is a way of implementing tracking, not a way of escaping it.
- It adds the calibration/resolution distinction, the indication/description split, and the point that human feelings of knowing are paradigmatically proxy-based (Koriat; Reder and Ritter). The last disarms the 'not real monitoring' reply without a double standard.

A engages the core philosophical literature more directly. B, however, advances the debate further: its distinctions are new, they are non-trivial, and they make the question tractable rather than merely reopening it.

Both essays make the same core point: the aetiology of a reporting disposition (training) does not settle what the report counterfactually depends on (mechanism). They also both note that a model imitating humans can instrumentally use its own states, which produces tracking. They differ in how much they add beyond that point.

A's contribution is mainly a skilful application of familiar tools to the debunking argument: Sober's selection-for versus selection-of, Nozick's method-relativized sensitivity, and the third-factor replies to Street. Its most original claim is that debunking strength varies inversely with causal proximity between target and mechanism. That claim is suggestive but overstated: causal integration makes tracking possible, not likely, so self-report being 'the limiting case' does little to lower the debunker's prior. The M1/M2 case usefully exposes why 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' is ill-posed. The repaired criterion (intervention, content-match, non-observational route) is close to Lindsey's existing operationalization and adds little.

B builds a positive framework that is more precise and more original.
(i) The derivation of inherited allocation A_D(x) shows exactly what a human corpus can and cannot fix: allocation over prompts at a typical author's rate, never dependence on the model's own state m.
(ii) The four-grain taxonomy is genuinely new. The dispositional self-theory option (H2) shows the trained/tracking dichotomy is neither exclusive nor exhaustive. Each hypothesis is paired with a test that discriminates it: stratification on A_D, sibling and observer comparisons, item-level editing, and proxy dissociation.
(iii) The common-cause objection is diagnosed precisely. The fork must be realized inside the network, so 'corpus frequency is a common cause' is one answer to a mediation question, not an alternative to it.
(iv) Further distinctions sharpen the analysis: calibration versus resolution (via Murphy's decomposition), indication versus description, and proxy monitoring as the human norm (Koriat; Reder & Ritter).

B also handles the regression dilemma and the off-manifold worry more rigorously than A handles its analogues. A is more embedded in the metaethics debunking literature. B, however, turns the dissolution into a falsifiable, finer-grained research program and offers more conceptual distinctions of lasting value. That makes it the more valuable contribution.

Both essays converge on the same core insight: training aetiology does not settle whether a report counterfactually depends on the state it describes, so the question turns on mechanism and intervention. B develops that insight further, and with fewer argumentative gaps.

**Strengths of A.** A's philosophical apparatus is genuinely good. It recasts debunking as a likelihood-ratio and screening-off claim, applies Sober's selection-for/selection-of distinction, uses Nozick's method-relativization, and argues that debunking strength is inversely related to causal proximity. That last thesis has reach beyond AI. Its M1/M2 point, that one cannot hold the 'mimicry pathway' fixed when imitation may be implemented by self-monitoring, is sharp.

**Weaknesses of A.** Its constructive payoff is thin. The repaired criterion (intervention, content-match, non-observational route) is close to what the objection already proposed. The causal-proximity argument also moves quickly from 'the states are constituents of the mechanism' to 'nothing stands in the way of tracking.'

**Why B is stronger.** It builds a more original and more productive framework:
- A formal derivation of 'inherited allocation' A_D(x), showing exactly what the human corpus can and cannot fix. The model's own state never appears in it.
- A careful diagnosis of the common-cause objection: the fork must be realized inside the network, so 'corpus frequency is a common cause' is one answer to a mediation question, not an alternative to it.
- Murphy's calibration/resolution decomposition, used to separate stylistic base-rate effects from allocation evidence.
- A four-way taxonomy of causal grain (inherited allocation, self-theory, proxy monitoring, direct monitoring). It shows 'trained vs. tracking' is neither exclusive nor exhaustive, and identifies dispositional self-theory as a distinct, trained-yet-tracking category.
- Discriminating test designs that map onto these hypotheses: stratifying on A_D, sibling and observer comparisons, item-level edits, and proxy dissociation.

B also handles the regression dilemma more rigorously, arguing for specificity over mere residual covariance, intervention over observation, and on-manifold controls. Its human parallels are more precise: Koriat's accessibility account and Reder & Ritter's familiarity findings as paradigm proxy monitoring. And its reference/description distinction (a report can be a good indicator but a poor description) is a valuable clarification absent from A.

**Verdict.** A has broader philosophical connective tissue. B makes the more substantive and durable contribution, turning a contested dilemma into a well-specified classification problem with principled criteria for resolving it.

The two essays are close. Both are strong and partly overlap: A's §3 'twist' and B's M2 case make the same point, that imitation can be implemented by self-monitoring. A is the better methods paper. Its derivation of inherited allocation A_D, its H1–H4 taxonomy of causal grain (especially H2, self-theory as tracking of a dispositional fact), its use of Murphy's calibration/resolution decomposition, and its stratification, sibling/observer and editing tests are concrete and largely original. But much of A's value is empirical design rather than philosophical knowledge, and its philosophical core is lightly argued. That core is the aetiology/grain distinction, backed by a thermometer and a child analogy. B's contributions travel further. First, it shows that the debunker's evidential conclusion just is a screening-off claim (L_T = 1), and that screening off need not require fixation. Second, it uses Sober's selection-for/selection-of distinction to locate the invalid step from 'the objective does not mention self-tracking' to 'the mechanism does not track.' Third, it argues that the debunker's counterfactual must be method-relativized in Nozick's sense; relativized, it becomes an empirical claim about mechanism, and unrelativized, it would debunk human self-report too. Fourth, and most novel, it explains why Street-style coarse debunking works in metaethics: the target facts are causally isolated. It infers that debunking power varies inversely with causal proximity, so self-report is the worst possible case for the debunker. This links the AI self-report debate to evolutionary debunking and sensitivity theory in a way that transfers to other domains. B also handles the human asymmetry more precisely: a developmental loop runs through the subject's own states, and losing it lowers the prior without defeating the evidence. Finally, B exposes a substantive error in the interventionist test as usually stated, since 'holding the mimicry pathway fixed' misclassifies M2. On balance, B makes the more valuable contribution to philosophical knowledge, while A is the more valuable contribution to research methodology.

Both essays are strong and reach a similar destination: the 'trained, therefore not tracking' inference fails, and whether a report tracks its referent is a mechanism-level question settled by intervention. B makes the more valuable philosophical contribution because it diagnoses the general structure of the skeptic's error and connects it to established debates. A mainly builds an empirical research programme.

B's specific contributions:
(i) It shows that the debunker's evidential conclusion (likelihood ratio = 1) just is a screening-off claim. This unifies the probabilistic and genealogical framings rather than letting the skeptic switch between them.
(ii) It applies Sober's selection-for/selection-of distinction and Nozick's method-relativized sensitivity condition. Together these locate one equivocation, between why a disposition was selected and how a report is produced, across the probabilistic, debunking and counterfactual versions of the argument.
(iii) It offers a genuinely new comparative thesis: coarse genealogical debunking works in metaethics because Street's targets are causally isolated from every candidate mechanism. Its force therefore varies inversely with causal proximity, and self-report sits at the integrated extreme. The epiphenomenalist rejoinder is correctly redirected to Chalmers's paradox of phenomenal judgment, so it cannot generate a human/model asymmetry.
(iv) The M1/M2 case shows that the referee's test, 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed', presupposes that imitation and introspection are distinct causal pathways. That presupposition misclassifies a network whose imitation is implemented by self-monitoring. This is a precise correction to an interventionist formulation that is likely to be widely used.
(v) Its treatment of the human asymmetry is candid and precise. In children, the public proxies used for correction are caused by the subject's own states. The asymmetry is conceded, but shown to lower priors rather than defeat evidence, and to be contingent on post-training practice.

A's merits are real:
- The derivation of inherited allocation A_D(x) as a function of x alone.
- The aetiology/grain distinction.
- The H1–H4 taxonomy. H2, dispositional self-theory that is both trained and tracking, is a nice distinction.
- Murphy's split between calibration and resolution, which isolates what allocation evidence is.
- The point that any corpus-frequency fork must be realized inside the network, making 'common cause' an answer to a mediation question rather than an alternative to it.
- The Koriat and Reder & Ritter parallel, showing proxy monitoring is the human standard.

A's limitations relative to B:
- Its philosophical core (aetiology does not cancel counterfactual dependence; thermometer and child analogies) is fairly quickly stated and draws on Dretske and Woodward without much development.
- Much of its length is experimental design (T1–T4, off-manifold controls) that largely systematizes existing ML work: Kadavath, Binder, Ferrando, Lindsey.
- Its 'twist' in §3 and its shared-representation reply in §6 make essentially the same point as B's M1/M2 case, but without B's diagnosis of why the skeptic's pathway-separation assumption fails in general.
- It confines itself to factual-uncertainty reports. B's framework covers the debunking argument as such.

B has weaknesses too:
- The inverse-proximity thesis is asserted rather than defended against naturalist debunkers, such as those who target moral beliefs even granting naturalism.
- Its three-part criterion inherits unresolved questions about individuating 'the state the report is about'.

On balance, B's arguments are more general, more transferable to adjacent debates, and more clearly philosophical in kind, so its contribution is the more valuable.

Both essays reach a similar core thesis: the fact that a reporting disposition was produced by training does not settle whether the report depends on the state it is about, and the question must be answered by mechanism-level intervention. They differ in how much philosophical work they do to get there.

Essay B makes the more valuable contribution, for four reasons.

1. It recasts the training worry as genealogical debunking. Via the likelihood ratio, it shows that the debunker's evidential conclusion just is a screening-off claim.

2. It locates the decisive equivocation precisely, using two established tools: Sober's distinction between selection-for and selection-of, and Nozick's method-relativization of sensitivity. Debunking needs a premise about how the report is produced. It is entitled only to a premise about why the disposition was selected.

3. Its most original move, in section 5, explains why Street-style coarse debunking works in metaethics. The target facts there are causally isolated from every candidate mechanism. Debunking therefore weakens as target facts become causally integrated, and self-report is the limiting case, since the reported states are constituents of the reporting mechanism. This is a generalizable claim that matters beyond the AI case. It also blocks the epiphenomenalist rejoinder by noting that this rejoinder no longer depends on training.

4. The M1/M2 case shows that the objector's own test, intervening while 'holding the mimicry pathway fixed', presupposes the false dichotomy at issue. Imitation describes behaviour; introspection describes mechanism; one can implement the other. This yields a corrected interventionist criterion with intervention, content-match and non-observational conditions. The treatment of the human asymmetry (public proxies are caused by the subject's own states) is also more precise than Essay A's handling of human parallels.

Essay A has real strengths:
- the derivation of inherited allocation A_D from what the corpus records;
- the H1–H4 grain taxonomy, especially H2 'self-theory' and the observer test that isolates it;
- the point that a common-cause fork must be realized inside the network, so it is itself a mediation hypothesis;
- the calibration/resolution distinction.

These are often more fine-grained than anything in B. But they are largely an experimental-design programme for interpretability. Philosophically, A rests on the aetiology/dependence distinction, which it asserts via the thermometer and child analogies rather than argues for. Its insights stay local to LLM uncertainty reports, while B's results bear on debunking arguments generally. Weighed by contribution to philosophical knowledge, B edges out A.

Both essays are strong, and A is the more tightly argued. Its use of the likelihood ratio to show that the debunker's conclusion just is a screening-off claim is clean. So is its pairing of Sober's selection-for/selection-of with Nozick's method-relativized sensitivity. Its observation that genealogical debunking weakens as the target facts become causally available to the belief-forming mechanism (strong against robust moral realism, weak for self-report) is a genuinely useful structural point. The M1/M2 case also identifies a real flaw in the 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' test. Still, A is mainly a refutation: it shows that the coarse training argument cannot deliver an a priori defeater and hands the question to interventionist empirical work. Much of its machinery (third-factor replies, method-relativity, Woodwardian intervention) applies existing tools in a familiar way.

B contributes more new, contestable, and productive philosophy. First, it separates symptomatic from testimonial evidence. It then argues that synchronic covariance and counterfactual sensitivity cannot single out which state a report concerns, which brings the indeterminacy problem from informational semantics into the epistemology of AI self-report. That challenges the interventionist framing A ends with, since A's criterion presupposes that 'the state the report is about' is already fixed.

Second, the Dretskean anchor condition, with gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, maintenance, and resolution, is a substantive positive account. It yields concrete, testable consequences:
- Base-model first-person reports are anchored to the modelled speaker or persona, not to the model. This gives the role-play picture a principled basis and makes a checkable prediction.
- A co-production failure mode in probe-anchored training shows perfect synchronic covariance without testimony. This is new and directly relevant to how such training should be designed.
- Lindsey's results split into an anchored concept term and an unanchored meta-report, which predicts the observed asymmetry in robustness.
- Nisbett & Wilson, choice blindness, and Schwitzgebel's cases are reinterpreted as failures of anchoring or resolution, turning apparent counterexamples into support.

B has weaknesses:
- The clock case leans on stipulation.
- The Swampman treatment is strained.
- Its claim that base-model reports cannot be anchored to the model's own states sits uneasily with A's common-cause argument about uncertainty. B's own common-cause clause should allow that, and B does not address it.
- 'Default entitlement' modelled on Burge is asserted more than argued.

Even so, B advances a novel framework with greater explanatory reach and more distinctive commitments. A mostly clears ground and points to empirical work. On contribution to knowledge, B edges ahead.

Both essays are competent and draw on much of the same literature, but B makes the larger and more original contribution.

What A achieves. A's main achievement is diagnostic. It shows that the 'training explanation' equivocates between why a disposition was selected and how a report is produced, using:
- Sober's selection-for/selection-of distinction;
- Nozick's method-relativization of sensitivity;
- a neat point that coarse genealogical debunking (Street) works only when the target facts are causally isolated from the belief-forming mechanism, so self-report is the least favourable case for it.
The M1/M2 case is A's best moment. It shows that 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' is ill-posed when the imitation is implemented by self-monitoring.

Limits of A. Much of A recombines established moves: third-factor replies, method-relativity, and Woodwardian interventionism applied to Lindsey-style experiments. Its conclusion is modest and largely negative: no a priori defeater, lower priors, go and test. Its repaired criterion also presupposes the very thing at issue. It restricts S to 'the state the report is about' but gives no account of what fixes which state that is.

What B adds. B attacks exactly that gap and builds a positive theory.
- It distinguishes testimonial from symptomatic evidence and argues that synchronic covariance is many-many, so it cannot fix the target of a self-report.
- It then offers a Dretske/Godfrey-Smith-style anchor condition, with gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, maintenance, and resolution, applied to an epistemic question about self-report vocabulary.

The framework yields several genuinely new and productive results:
- The clock case shows that gate correlation without the right causal structure anchors the wrong content.
- The co-production case shows that probe-trained reports can satisfy covariance and sensitivity perfectly yet fail to be testimony. This has a concrete methodological upshot for anchoring training.
- Base-model first-person reports come out as anchored to the modelled speaker or persona rather than to the model itself. This gives a principled, testable version of the role-play picture and is more informative than 'mere mimicry'.
- It gives a unified reading of the human unreliability data. Nisbett and Wilson and choice blindness fall in an unanchored process-vocabulary domain, and Schwitzgebel's cases concern resolution beyond what the gates discriminated.
- It explains why etiology matters epistemically when the target cannot be independently measured.

Limits of B. B has contestable points:
- The testimony/symptom line may be too sharp.
- Its reading of Lindsey is somewhat speculative.
- The Swampman discussion is brief.

Verdict. B's weaknesses are those of an ambitious new framework. A's are those of a careful but more derivative rebuttal. B advances the debate further, both conceptually and in the empirical predictions it generates.

Both essays are competent replies to a strong referee objection, but B makes the more substantive positive contribution.

A's contribution is largely deflationary. It shows that genealogical debunking cannot reach model self-reports from the training objective alone, and leaves the question to mechanism-level testing. Its best moves are real:
- Sober's selection-for/selection-of distinction, applied to gradient descent.
- Nozick's method-relativization of sensitivity.
- The observation that coarse debunking strengthens as the target becomes causally isolated, so self-report is its weakest case.
- The M1/M2 case, showing that 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' misfires when mimicry is implemented by self-monitoring.

But the conclusion (no a priori defeater, lower prior, test by intervention) is close to where much of the literature already sits. Its interventionist criterion also has a gap. The 'content-match' condition presupposes that we have already fixed which state a report is about, and A gives no account of how that is fixed.

B addresses exactly that gap, and offers a positive, falsifiable theory. Its distinctive contributions are:
- **Testimony versus symptom.** It distinguishes testimonial from symptomatic evidence and argues that, where the target state is not independently measurable, synchronic covariance cannot even fix the target.
- **A worked-out anchor condition.** It adapts Dretske and Godfrey-Smith into gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, maintenance, and resolution.
- **A diagnosis of base models.** Base-model self-reports come out as anchored to the modeled persona, not to the model. This gives a principled grounding for the role-play view and yields testable predictions.
- **The co-production case.** It shows a purely synchronic reliability criterion would certify reports produced in the wrong causal direction. This is a practically important point about training against probes.
- **A unified reading of the confabulation literature.** Nisbett and Wilson, choice blindness, Schwitzgebel and alexithymia become a single pattern: anchor failure, or the limits of resolution and maintenance.
- **A finer reading of Lindsey.** It separates the anchored concept term from the unanchored meta-report, predicting robust identification but fragile anomaly detection.

B has contestable commitments:
- Its teleosemantic treatment of Swampman is contested.
- It may overstate the claim that testimony requires an etiological anchor.
- The clock case relies on particular assumptions about learning.

Even so, it generates more novel distinctions, explanations and predictions, and engages a deeper problem (content fixation) than A's carefully argued but more expected rebuttal.

Both essays are serious, but A contributes more new philosophy. It proposes a positive theory and backs it with distinctions and cases that do real work. The core move is to separate symptomatic from testimonial evidence. A then argues that synchronic covariance cannot fix which of the many states a report is sensitive to is the one it concerns. This brings the indeterminacy problem from informational semantics (Fodor, Dretske, Millikan) to bear on AI self-report in a fresh way. It also explains why etiology matters for content and not merely as a reliability indicator. Several moves are novel: (1) the clock case, showing that correlation at the gate does not anchor; (2) the co-production case, where gradients let the report shape the probed feature, which satisfies every synchronic covariance and sensitivity condition yet is not testimony; (3) the diagnosis that base-model self-reports are anchored to the modelled persona, a testable sharpening of the role-play view; (4) the rereading of Nisbett and Wilson as exactly the domain where human vocabulary was never anchored, with Schwitzgebel's cases explained by anchor resolution; (5) splitting Lindsey's results into an anchored concept term and unanchored meta-content, which yields a differential prediction. A has weak points. Its persona-anchoring claim for base models is too quick, since A1 permits common-cause structures that could anchor some terms, such as uncertainty, to the model's own states. The claim that unanchored content is 'idle' is also contestable. B is tight and dialectically clean. Its strongest contributions are the M1/M2 case, which shows that 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' assumes a false dichotomy, and the observation that coarse genealogical debunking depends on the target facts being causally isolated. But much of B rests on familiar tools: Sober's selection-for versus selection-of, Nozick's method-relativity, and third-factor replies to Street. Its repaired criterion largely restates the grounding and internality conditions already in Lindsey and in Comșa and Shanahan. Its conclusion, that there is no default entitlement and mechanism-level evidence is needed, is more modest and closer to existing consensus. A advances a distinctive and contestable thesis with new conceptual machinery, so its contribution is greater.

Both essays are strong, but A contributes more original and constructive philosophy. Its anchor condition has three parts: gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, and maintenance, plus a notion of resolution. Together with the distinction between symptomatic and testimonial evidence, this gives a positive account of when self-reports are evidence through their content. That goes beyond B's mainly negative result that the training explanation fails as an a priori defeater. Several of A's moves are genuinely new and do real work. The clock case shows that correlation at the gate does not anchor reference; causal structure does. The co-production case shows a direction-of-causation requirement that a purely synchronic covariance criterion cannot capture. The diagnosis that base-model first-person reports are anchored to the modelled persona rather than the model gives the role-play picture a principled basis and yields testable predictions. A also reinterprets Nisbett & Wilson, Schwitzgebel, and alexithymia as cases of anchor failure or insufficient resolution, which turns the skeptic's counterexamples into support. The target-fixation argument against the synchronic view draws properly on the indeterminacy problem in informational semantics. B is tightly argued and has real insights: the likelihood-ratio reconstruction, Sober's selection-for versus selection-of distinction, method-relativized sensitivity, the claim that debunking weakens with causal proximity, and the M1/M2 case showing the mimicry pathway cannot be held fixed. But B largely assembles established tools (Sober, Nozick, Woodward, third-factor replies to Street) to defend a modest conclusion. Its repaired interventionist criterion is close to the referee's own proposal. A has weaknesses too. Its testimonial/symptomatic distinction is contestable, and the Swampman concession strains it. Still, A advances a more distinctive, systematic, and empirically fruitful thesis.

Both essays are strong. B makes the more secure and more general contribution, while A's more ambitious positive theory has an internal tension it does not resolve.

B's contributions:
(1) It shows, via the likelihood ratio, that the genealogical debunker's evidential conclusion just is a screening-off claim. This unifies the probabilistic and debunking framings instead of conceding that they differ.
(2) It uses Sober's selection-for versus selection-of distinction and Nozick's method-relativization to locate a single equivocation that recurs across the argument's probabilistic, debunking and counterfactual forms: why a disposition was selected versus how a report is produced. Coarse objective-level premises cannot yield the mechanism-level conclusion that debunking needs.
(3) It explains why Street-style debunking can run at the coarse level in metaethics: the target facts are causally isolated from every candidate mechanism. From this it derives a general principle that debunking force varies inversely with causal proximity, which places self-report at the most favorable extreme. This is a portable insight beyond the AI case.
(4) Its M1/M2 case shows that 'hold the mimicry pathway fixed' builds in a false dichotomy, because imitation can be implemented by self-monitoring. The case also yields a repaired interventionist criterion that discriminates correctly.
Its concessions (no default entitlement, lower priors, divergent-prediction tests) are calibrated and well motivated.

A is more original in places: the testimonial/symptomatic distinction, the target-fixation argument against purely synchronic accounts, the clock and co-production cases, and the re-reading of Nisbett and Wilson as an unanchored domain. But its central claim does not hold up well against B's common-cause point. A allows common-cause anchoring (it uses this to explain 'bread' in Lindsey) yet asserts that base-model self-reports are anchored only to persona representations. Nothing excludes the model's own uncertainty serving as the common-cause-linked state, as in B's M2 case. A's case for a default testimonial entitlement and for generalization beyond calibration also leans on stipulation and on unverified empirical hopes.

On balance, B's arguments are tighter, rest more securely on established tools, and yield more robust and generalizable conclusions.

Both essays are strong. B's contribution is more philosophically substantive and less purely methodological.

Strengths of A:
- A is the more rigorous essay. The split of allocation into inherited allocation A_D and model-specific dependence is careful.
- The four grain hypotheses (H1–H4) and the tests T1–T4 are well designed.
- The reply to the common-cause objection is sharp: the fork must be realized inside the network, so the objection becomes a mediation question.
- Bringing in Murphy's calibration/resolution decomposition is a genuine clarification.

Limits of A:
- Much of A's philosophical payload is a fairly familiar point, that aetiology does not undercut counterfactual dependence (Dretske, Woodward, the thermometer case).
- The rest is an experimental programme for functional states whose target variable m* the experimenter fixes in advance.
- By its own admission, A says little about the reports that motivate the debate: affect and experience, where no m* can be specified.

Strengths of B:
- B introduces a real distinction between symptomatic and testimonial evidence.
- It identifies a problem the synchronic-reliability view cannot handle, which A implicitly faces too: target fixation. Covariance is many-many, and only calibration or a content-fixing history settles which state a report is about.
- It recruits Dretske's learning-based metasemantics and Godfrey-Smith's modern-history functions to supply an epistemic anchor condition. The condition comes with a gate-linkage requirement, a direction-of-causation requirement and a resolution parameter.
- Several results do real work:
  - The clock case shows that correlation at the gate is insufficient.
  - The co-production case shows that perfect synchronic covariance can fail to be testimony. This is a novel and important point for probe-based training proposals like Perez & Long.
  - The diagnosis that base-model self-reports are anchored to the modelled persona gives the role-play view a principled footing.
  - The reinterpretations of Binder et al., Lindsey, Nisbett & Wilson, Schwitzgebel and alexithymia as anchor failures or resolution limits are illuminating and testable.

Weaknesses of B:
- The clock case is somewhat stipulative.
- The Swampman treatment is quick.
- The claim that symptomatic evidence always requires target calibration could be contested.

On balance, B advances the conceptual question of when self-reports can be taken at their word, especially where targets are unmeasurable. That is the question that matters for AI welfare and sentience, and it is the more valuable contribution to philosophical knowledge.

Both essays are strong replies to a referee's objection, but B makes the deeper and more distinctively philosophical contribution.

A's strengths and limits. A's lexicon/allocation split, its derivation of inherited allocation A_D, and its H1–H4 taxonomy with discriminating tests (T1–T4) are rigorous and empirically sophisticated. Its best philosophical move is reframing the common-cause objection as a mediation hypothesis that must be realized inside the network. But its core thesis is fairly standard Dretske/Woodward. Aetiology does not undercut counterfactual dependence, and evidential import is fixed by which variable a report depends on. Much of the remaining value is experimental design, close to a philosophy-of-science methods note. A also explicitly confines itself to functional states like retrieval failure, where an independent target variable m* can be specified. It concedes that where no m* exists, which includes affect and the morally salient reports, its framework yields only 'unestablished.'

Why B goes further. B tackles that harder case directly. Its distinction between symptomatic and testimonial evidence shows that synchronic covariance cannot fix which of many co-varying states a report is about. This connects to the disjunction and distality problems in informational semantics. B also explains why calibration-based evidence is unavailable exactly when the target is not independently measurable. Its anchor condition (gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, maintenance, resolution) is a Dretskean recruitment account put to novel epistemic use. Several results are genuinely new:
- The clock case shows that correlation at the gate does not anchor.
- The co-production case shows that perfect synchronic covariance can run in the wrong causal direction, so a purely synchronic criterion is insufficient.
- Base-model self-reports are diagnosed as anchored to the modeled persona rather than to the model. This gives a principled grounding for the role-play picture and a testable prediction.
- Binder et al. and Lindsey are reread as confirming the view. The concept term is anchored by pretraining while the meta-content is not, which predicts the observed fragility of anomaly detection.
- Nisbett–Wilson, choice blindness, and Schwitzgebel become cases of absent anchoring or insufficient resolution rather than counterexamples.

B's weaknesses. Several moves are underspecified:
- The common-cause clause in (A1) is vague. It is unclear why the scheduled-treatment case is excluded 'in the way that matters.'
- The Swampman discussion borrows an anchor somewhat ad hoc.
- The entitlement analogy to Burge's perceptual entitlement is asserted more than defended.

Verdict. A is more methodologically airtight. B engages the central contested questions: content determination, the epistemology of testimony, and debunking. It also yields more novel and transferable philosophical insight.

Both essays are strong replies to the same deflationary worry. B makes the more distinctively philosophical contribution, while A makes the more rigorous methodological one.

A's main moves are sound and carefully executed:
- It splits self-report behaviour into lexicon and allocation, and derives an inherited allocation A_D from the corpus-generating process.
- It separates aetiology from causal grain, using Dretske and Woodward.
- It shows that the common-cause objection is really a mediation hypothesis that interventions can settle.
- It uses Murphy's distinction between calibration and resolution.

But most of A's payoff is an empirical research programme (H1–H4, T1–T4). Its central philosophical claim, that being trained is compatible with counterfactual dependence on the reported state, is close to what an informational or interventionist theorist would already say. A also largely assumes that the target variable m* can be fixed for each predicate. It does not ask what makes a report *about* m* rather than some other correlated variable.

B confronts exactly that question, and it yields several new results:
- It distinguishes symptomatic from testimonial evidence, and argues that synchronic covariance is a many-many relation that cannot fix a report's target.
- It offers a structured anchor condition: gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, and maintenance, plus a notion of resolution. It grounds this in Dretske (1988) and Godfrey-Smith's modern-history view.
- The clock case shows that correlation at the gate does not anchor; causal structure does.
- The co-production case is a sharp counterexample to purely synchronic reliability criteria.
- It argues that base-model first-person reports are anchored to a persona or speaker representation, not to the model itself. This is a novel, testable diagnosis that makes the role-play picture principled.
- It reinterprets Nisbett and Wilson, choice blindness, Schwitzgebel and alexithymia as failures of the anchor (or of its resolution or maintenance), which turns the objector's counterexamples into support.
- It reads Binder et al. and Lindsey in a way that yields differential predictions: concept identification should be robust, anomaly detection fragile.

B has real vulnerabilities:
- It leans on contested teleosemantic answers to the problem of fixing content.
- The claim that testimony needs no calibration by the hearer is asserted more than argued.
- Its handling of Swampman is quick.

Even so, B's distinctions do more new conceptual work on whether AI self-reports can be testimony, and B identifies a problem, target fixation, that A's framework presupposes away.

Both essays are strong. A makes the deeper and more original philosophical contribution, while B is the more rigorous and more empirically actionable piece.

A's central move separates testimonial evidence (evidence through content, usable without calibrating against the target) from symptomatic evidence. It pairs this with a target-fixation argument: synchronic covariance is a many-many relation and cannot settle which state a report concerns. This addresses a gap that purely reliabilist or interventionist treatments, B's included, leave open. B simply stipulates the target variable m* and concedes that for affect reports there may be none.

A's anchor condition (gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, maintenance, resolution) applies Dretskean and teleosemantic resources to self-report vocabulary, and it pays off several times over:
- The clock case shows that correlation at the gate is not what anchors.
- The co-production case is a clean counterexample to a covariance-plus-sensitivity criterion.
- It diagnoses base-model first-person reports as anchored to the modelled persona, a principled version of the role-play view that yields testable predictions.
- It unifies Nisbett and Wilson and choice blindness as unanchored process vocabulary, and Schwitzgebel's cases as failures of resolution.
- Its point about the epistemic value of testimony beyond measurable targets locates where the AI moral-status question actually bites.

A has real weaknesses. It inherits known problems with Dretske's learning-based semantics. The Swampman 'borrowed anchor' reply is strained. The claim that unanchored perfect covariance is merely symptomatic (the 'zorp' argument) is contestable.

B is sharper in several places:
- Its formal derivation of inherited allocation A_D.
- Its argument that a corpus-frequency fork must be realized inside the network, so that 'common cause' becomes a mediation hypothesis that interventions can test.
- Its use of Murphy's calibration/resolution decomposition.
- Its H1–H4 grain taxonomy with discriminating designs (T1–T4).

Much of B, however, is a skilful application of Woodward and Pearl style interventionism and existing metacognition research to a narrower domain, mainly factual uncertainty. Its headline claim that aetiology does not compete with dependence is fairly standard reliabilism. B is the better research programme. A advances the philosophical understanding of what makes a self-report evidence about its producer at all, so it makes the more valuable philosophical contribution.

Both essays are strong, but A makes the more distinctively philosophical contribution. Its central move is the distinction between symptomatic evidence, which needs calibration against the target, and testimonial evidence, which runs through content. This is tied to a teleosemantic argument (Dretske 1988; Godfrey-Smith's maintenance condition) that synchronic covariance cannot fix which of many states a report concerns. A sharpens this with well-chosen cases. The clock case shows that correlation at the gate is not enough. The co-production case shows that perfect synchronic covariance in the wrong causal direction is not testimony, which a purely synchronic criterion cannot exclude. A also yields a precise diagnosis: base-model self-reports are anchored to the modelled persona, not to the model. This gives a principled grounding for the role-play picture of Shanahan et al. and a testable prediction. A reinterprets Binder et al., Nisbett & Wilson and Schwitzgebel as confirming instances, via the resolution and process-report points, and these readings are illuminating rather than ad hoc. Crucially, A addresses the hard case, targets that cannot be measured independently, such as affect, and explains why etiology matters epistemically there. B is rigorous and methodologically valuable. Its lexicon/allocation split, the derivation of inherited allocation A_D(x), and the four-way taxonomy of causal grain with tests T1–T4 are useful. So is its point that a corpus-frequency 'common cause' must be realized as a mediation structure inside the network. But its key philosophical claim, that aetiology does not compete with counterfactual dependence, is fairly standard (Dretske 1981; Woodward). Its main payoff is an experimental design for functional states such as retrieval failure. B explicitly concedes it yields no verdict where no first-order variable m* can be specified, which is precisely where A's account does its work. A has weaknesses. Its insistence that testimonial standing requires anchoring may be contestable, and its handling of Lindsey (2025) is partly speculative. Even so, A advances the epistemology and metasemantics of self-report more substantially, while B mainly advances methodology.

This is a close call; I prefer A, but a referee who prizes methodological rigor could reasonably reverse it. A's advantage is philosophical depth and originality. It separates symptomatic from testimonial evidence and argues that synchronic covariance cannot fix which of a network's many co-varying states a report is about (the target-fixation problem). It then imports Dretske/Godfrey-Smith learning-based metasemantics as a three-part 'anchor' condition: gate-linkage, learner-side recruitment, and maintenance, with resolution. The thesis does real explanatory work. It reclassifies base-model self-reports as testimony about the modelled persona, which gives a principled form of the role-play view. It locates Nisbett & Wilson and choice blindness in an unanchored process-report vocabulary and reads Schwitzgebel's cases as failures of anchor resolution. It also identifies a direction-of-causation (co-production) failure that a purely synchronic reliability criterion cannot exclude. Most importantly, it engages the hard case B sets aside: targets that cannot be independently measured, where calibration-based evidence is unavailable. A has real weaknesses. Its readings of Lindsey and Nisbett & Wilson look post hoc. Its claim that testimony needs no calibration is shaky, since knowing that an anchor holds is plausibly a structural form of calibration. The Swampman 'borrowed anchor' move is thin. B is more rigorous and empirically tractable. Its formal derivation of 'inherited allocation' A_D(x), its point that a corpus-frequency confounder must be realized as a fork inside the network, the H1–H4 causal-grain taxonomy with the T1–T4 discriminating designs, the calibration/resolution distinction via Murphy, and the Koriat proxy-monitoring parallel are all valuable. But its core philosophical claim, that aetiology does not settle evidential dependence, is a fairly standard reliabilist/interventionist point. Its main contribution is a well-built experimental-design framework restricted to functional states such as uncertainty. A therefore offers the more distinctive and deeper philosophical thesis, while B is the stronger methodological piece.
